The empirical section is broader than many UQ papers, covering synthetic conditional-coverage experiments, 17 real-world tabular datasets, multiple metrics, multiple model variants, and a PCS-style case study.

The paper is mostly well organized and acknowledges key caveats, including computational overhead, estimator quality dependence, and the lack of strict finite-sample guarantees for the main implementation.
Appendix comparisons and ablations, including fixed-lambda/fixed-gamma variants and UACQR-style baselines, help isolate the benefit of adaptive reweighting.
weaknesses: The core methodological novelty is limited: learning two scalar weights for a linear combination of uncertainty components is a natural calibration extension, and the positioning against closely related calibrated ensemble, Bayesian, and UACQR-style methods is not strong enough to establish a clearly new conceptual advance.

The main implementation reuses the same validation/calibration data to select models, tune lambda over a large grid, and calibrate gamma, so the standard finite-sample conformal guarantee does not apply; the conformalized variant with a separate calibration split is only presented theoretically and is not the main evaluated method.

The theoretical result is weak and largely asymptotic: under consistency of the aleatoric quantile estimator, epistemic uncertainty vanishes and the interval converges to true conditional quantiles. This does not substantially explain finite-sample gains from CLEAR or provide meaningful conditional-coverage guarantees.

The empirical claims about improved conditional coverage are mainly supported by synthetic extrapolation plots; the real-world benchmark reports marginal test coverage and interval/loss metrics, but does not evaluate subgroup/conditional coverage or distribution shift in a convincing way.

The main-paper baselines are mostly the method's own components. Stronger and more prominent comparisons to close alternatives, such as UACQR, local/adaptive conformal methods, calibrated deep ensembles, Bayesian uncertainty methods, and modern tabular probabilistic predictors, would be needed for a top-tier acceptance case.

Because CLEAR has an additional validation-optimized degree of freedom and uses a dense lambda grid, the comparison may favor CLEAR unless baselines receive equally careful tuning or the separate validation/calibration protocol is evaluated.

Some claims are overstated, especially phrases such as rigorously maintaining nominal coverage and achieving improved conditional coverage, given the acknowledged data reuse and the absence of finite-sample conditional guarantees.

Reproducibility is reasonable at the algorithmic level but incomplete from the manuscript alone: code is only referred to as supplementary, and implementation choices such as model selection, hyperparameters, and failed runs introduce complexity that may affect replication.
